claims.claim: Homozygous offspring of Oxtrflox/flox and Cyp19a1-Cre lines showed loss of preference to investigate female bedding.
claims.source: In contrast, the homozygous offspring of these two lines, which have impaired OXT signaling in aromatase-positive neurons, showed loss of preference to investigate female bedding (n = 13; male bedding = 59.0 ± 8.7 s, female bedding = 58.4 ± 5.9 s; p=0.95, t test; preference score = 0.02 ± 0.08, significantly lower than that of Oxtrflox/flox and Cyp19a1-Cre, p<0.05, t test; Figure 2G).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data presented in Figure 2G.

claims.claim: Male mice with impaired OXT signaling in aromatase-positive or TRH positive neurons still spent significantly longer durations in the goal chamber with the attractive cue than the goal chamber containing fox urine.
claims.source: Consistent with the apparently normal ability of Oxt-/- male mice to detect predator cues, male mice with impaired OXT signaling in aromatase-positive (Food zone = 82.7 ± 14.0 s, Food +fox urine zone = 51.8 ± 8.8 s; p<0.05, t test; n = 10) or TRH positive neurons (Female chamber = 65.8 ± 9.7 s, Fox urine zone = 41.1 ± 6.3 s; p<0.05, t test; n = 11) still spent significantly longer durations in the goal chamber with the attractive cue of either food or female urine than the goal chamber containing fox urine (Figure 2E and Figure 2F).

claims.claim: Aromatase-positive neurons represent a critical site for OXT action in the control of chemosensory discrimination of male versus female conspecifics.

claims.claim: Mice with specific impairment of OXT signaling in the MeA displayed loss of preference for female chemostimuli.
claims.source: We found that mice with specific impairment of OXT signaling in the MeA displayed loss of preference for female chemostimuli (male bedding = 40.8 ± 3.8 s, female bedding = 47.6 ± 5.7 s; p=0.29, multiple t-tests; preference score = 0.04 ± 0.05, n = 24), whereas control (GFP in MeA: male bedding = 25.7 ± 2.6 s, female bedding = 52.9 ± 6.8 s; p<0.01, t test; preference score = 0.32 ± 0.06, n = 10; GFP in BNST: male bedding = 31.6 ± 4.7 s, female bedding = 71.7 ± 9.9 s; p<0.01, t test; preference score = 0.36 ± 0.08, n = 10) and male mice with impaired OXT signaling in the BNST (GFP in MeA: male bedding = 28.4 ± 2.8 s, female bedding = 79.0 ± 9.6 s; p<0.001, t test; preference score = 0.42 ± 0.05, n = 18) presented normal preference in investigating female bedding (Figure 3B–G).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data presented in Figure 3B-G.

claims.claim: Male mice with impaired OXT signaling in the BNST presented normal preference in investigating female bedding.
claims.source: We found that mice with specific impairment of OXT signaling in the MeA displayed loss of preference for female chemostimuli (male bedding = 40.8 ± 3.8 s, female bedding = 47.6 ± 5.7 s; p=0.29, multiple t-tests; preference score = 0.04 ± 0.05, n = 24), whereas control (GFP in MeA: male bedding = 25.7 ± 2.6 s, female bedding = 52.9 ± 6.8 s; p<0.01, t test; preference score = 0.32 ± 0.06, n = 10; GFP in BNST: male bedding = 31.6 ± 4.7 s, female bedding = 71.7 ± 9.9 s; p<0.01, t test; preference score = 0.36 ± 0.08, n = 10) and male mice with impaired OXT signaling in the BNST (GFP in MeA: male bedding = 28.4 ± 2.8 s, female bedding = 79.0 ± 9.6 s; p<0.001, t test; preference score = 0.42 ± 0.05, n = 18) presented normal preference in investigating female bedding (Figure 3B–G).

claims.claim: Aromatase-positive neurons of the MeA, but not of the BNST, mediate the effect of OXT on the discrimination of sex-specific cues by male mice.

claims.claim: Rescue of OXTR expression in the MeA, but not the BNST, was sufficient to restore the preference for female chemostimuli in male mice.

claims.claim: Bilateral injection of AAV-OXTR to the MeA led to increased investigation of female bedding in mutant mice.
claims.source: Bilateral injection of AAV-OXTR to the MeA led to increased investigation of female bedding in mutant mice (male bedding = 35.7 ± 4.6 s, female bedding = 71.0 ± 6.9 s; p<0.01; t test; preference score = 0.33 ± 0.06, n = 13; Figure 3I–K), whereas virus-mediated OXTR expression in the BNST had no effect (male bedding = 35.3 ± 2.6 s, female bedding = 46.9 ± 4.0 s; p>0.05; t test; preference score = 0.13 ± 0.04, n = 21; Figure 3L–N).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data presented in Figure 3I-K.

claims.claim: Virus-mediated OXTR expression in the BNST had no effect on female bedding investigation in mutant mice.
claims.source: Bilateral injection of AAV-OXTR to the MeA led to increased investigation of female bedding in mutant mice (male bedding = 35.7 ± 4.6 s, female bedding = 71.0 ± 6.9 s; p<0.01; t test; preference score = 0.33 ± 0.06, n = 13; Figure 3I–K), whereas virus-mediated OXTR expression in the BNST had no effect (male bedding = 35.3 ± 2.6 s, female bedding = 46.9 ± 4.0 s; p>0.05; t test; preference score = 0.13 ± 0.04, n = 21; Figure 3L–N).

claims.claim: OXT signaling is required in MeApd aromatase-positive neurons for the discrimination of sex-specific cues.
claims.source: In summary, our data indicate that OXT signaling is required in MeApd aromatase-positive neurons for the discrimination of sex-specific cues.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the combined genetic, viral, and behavioral data.

claims.claim: The virus-mediated ablation and rescue of OXTR expression in adult MeA lead to corresponding changes in the ability of male mice to discriminate female and male conspecific cues.
claims.source: Although our results cannot rule out a possible role of OXT in configuring neural circuits regulating sex discrimination during development, the virus-mediated ablation and rescue of OXTR expression in adult MeA lead to corresponding changes in the ability of male mice to discriminate female and male conspecific cues, thus strongly suggesting that defects in chemosensory discrimination are a direct consequence of acute impairment of OXT signaling in the adult MeA.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the virus-mediated manipulation experiments in adult mice.

claims.claim: Defects in chemosensory discrimination are a direct consequence of acute impairment of OXT signaling in the adult MeA.
claims.source: Although our results cannot rule out a possible role of OXT in configuring neural circuits regulating sex discrimination during development, the virus-mediated ablation and rescue of OXTR expression in adult MeA lead to corresponding changes in the ability of male mice to discriminate female and male conspecific cues, thus strongly suggesting that defects in chemosensory discrimination are a direct consequence of acute impairment of OXT signaling in the adult MeA.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the virus-mediated manipulation experiments showing rapid behavioral changes.

claims.claim: In the absence of OXTR, MeA neurons display overall reduced responses to chemosensory cues.
claims.source: Our results showed that, in the absence of OXTR, MeA neurons display overall reduced responses to chemosensory cues, while the percentage of neurons responding to male cues is increased, suggesting that the lack of preference of OXT mutant mice for sex-specific cues results from abnormal patterns of MeA neural activity.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological recording data comparing control and mutant mice.

claims.claim: In the absence of OXTR, the percentage of MeA neurons responding to male cues is increased.
claims.source: Our results showed that, in the absence of OXTR, MeA neurons display overall reduced responses to chemosensory cues, while the percentage of neurons responding to male cues is increased, suggesting that the lack of preference of OXT mutant mice for sex-specific cues results from abnormal patterns of MeA neural activity.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological recording data comparing control and mutant mice.

claims.claim: The lack of preference of OXT mutant mice for sex-specific cues results from abnormal patterns of MeA neural activity.

claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the correlation between altered neural responses and behavioral phenotype.

claims.claim: Neuronal responses to mouse cues are reduced more than those to predator cues in OXT mutants.
claims.source: Moreover, consistent with a specific role of OXT in the processing of conspecific cues, neuronal responses to mouse cues are reduced more than those to predator cues in OXT mutants.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological recording data comparing responses to different stimuli.

claims.claim: Similar sex-preference behavioral defects are observed in constitutive as well as in conditionally virus-mediated OXTR ablation in the adult MeA.
claims.source: Our data showing that similar sex-preference behavioral defects are observed in constitutive as well as in conditionally virus-mediated OXTR ablation in the adult MeA strongly suggest a role for OXT signaling in adult.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by comparing behavioral phenotypes across different genetic and viral manipulations.

claims.claim: The effect of OXT mediated through OXTR in aromatase-expressing neurons is not developmental, but rather acts on a moment-to-moment basis even in adults.
claims.source: Therefore, the effect of OXT mediated through OXTR in aromatase-expressing neurons is not developmental, but rather acts on a moment-to-moment basis even in adults.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the acute effects observed with pharmacological and chemogenetic manipulations.

claims.claim: The establishment of the sexually dimorphic sensory representation in the MeA requires steroid signaling near the time of puberty.
claims.source: Our previous study showed that the establishment of the sexually dimorphic sensory representation in the MeA requires steroid signaling near the time of puberty to organize the functional representation of sensory stimuli (Bergan et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claims.claim: OXT-mediated acute modulation of MeA neuronal response can alter social behavior in the adult on a moment-to-moment basis, while maintaining the integrity of circuit connectivity.
claims.source: In contrast to the organizational effect of steroids, we found here that the OXT-mediated acute modulation of MeA neuronal response can alter social behavior in the adult on a moment-to-moment basis, while maintaining the integrity of circuit connectivity.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the acute effects of OXT manipulation on behavior and neural responses.

claims.claim: Social recognition is modulated by acute variation in OXT signaling.
claims.source: Social recognition is similarly modulated by acute variation in OXT signaling (Ferguson et al., 2001).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature on OXT and social recognition.

claims.claim: Specific activation of aromatase-expressing neurons in the MeA promotes aggressive behaviors.
claims.source: Recent studies have shown that specific activation of aromatase-expressing neurons in the MeA promotes aggressive behaviors (Unger et al., 2015), and that reproductive sensory cues are processed by both the MeApv (Ishii et al., 2017) and the MeApd (Bergan et al., 2014; Choi et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature on MeA aromatase neurons.

claims.claim: Reproductive sensory cues are processed by both the MeApv and the MeApd.
claims.source: Recent studies have shown that specific activation of aromatase-expressing neurons in the MeA promotes aggressive behaviors (Unger et al., 2015), and that reproductive sensory cues are processed by both the MeApv (Ishii et al., 2017) and the MeApd (Bergan et al., 2014; Choi et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature on MeA sensory processing.

claims.claim: OXT signaling through MeA aromatase-expressing neurons modulates the preference of male mice for interacting with female versus male mice.
claims.source: In further support of this view, our data show that OXT signaling through MeA aromatase-expressing neurons modulates the preference of male mice for interacting with female versus male mice, thus mediating a change in social preference that is likely to alter the balance of reproductive versus aggressive behaviors.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the behavioral and genetic data presented in the manuscript.

claims.claim: The change in sensory responses observed in the MeA parallels the changes observed in male social preference.
claims.source: The change in sensory responses observed in the MeA parallels the changes observed in male social preference, suggesting that the observed behavioral effect of OXT signaling is achieved by filtering which sensory responses have access to behavioral centers in the hypothalamus on a moment-to-moment basis.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the correlation between neural and behavioral changes.

claims.claim: The observed behavioral effect of OXT signaling is achieved by filtering which sensory responses have access to behavioral centers in the hypothalamus on a moment-to-moment basis.
claims.source: The change in sensory responses observed in the MeA parallels the changes observed in male social preference, suggesting that the observed behavioral effect of OXT signaling is achieved by filtering which sensory responses have access to behavioral centers in the hypothalamus on a moment-to-moment basis.

claims.claim: OXT enhances the responses of neurons in the MeA that encode female stimuli while suppressing sensory responses to both male and predator stimuli.
claims.source: We showed that OXT enhances the responses of neurons in the MeA that encode female stimuli while suppressing sensory responses to both male and predator stimuli.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological recording data showing differential effects on different stimulus types.

claims.claim: OXT is dynamically regulated by the external environment and an animal's internal physiological state.
claims.source: OXT is dynamically regulated by the external environment and an animal's internal physiological state (Devarajan and Rusak, 2004; Higashida et al., 2017; Kalin et al., 1985; Kendrick et al., 1986; Wathes et al., 1992), and the OXT-mediated filtering of sensory cues shown in our study likely supports a fine-tuning of behavioral responses according to the social context.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature on OXT regulation.

claims.claim: The OXT-mediated filtering of sensory cues likely supports a fine-tuning of behavioral responses according to the social context.
claims.source: OXT is dynamically regulated by the external environment and an animal's internal physiological state (Devarajan and Rusak, 2004; Higashida et al., 2017; Kalin et al., 1985; Kendrick et al., 1986; Wathes et al., 1992), and the OXT-mediated filtering of sensory cues shown in our study likely supports a fine-tuning of behavioral responses according to the social context.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the observed effects of OXT on sensory responses and behavior.

claims.claim: OXT has been shown to regulate specific brain functions by facilitating the release of other neurotransmitters, in particular dopamine and serotonin.
claims.source: OXT has been shown to regulate specific brain functions by facilitating the release of other neurotransmitters, in particular dopamine and serotonin (Dluzen et al., 2000; Dluzen et al., 1998; Dölen et al., 2013; Liu and Wang, 2003; Olazábal and Young, 2006; Ross et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature on OXT mechanisms.

claims.claim: OXT has been documented to increase neuronal firing rates, mainly, though not exclusively in fast-spiking interneurons.
claims.source: In addition OXT has been documented to increase neuronal firing rates, mainly, though not exclusively in fast-spiking interneurons, resulting in lower background activity and enhanced information transfer in cortical and non-cortical circuits (Marlin et al., 2015; Oettl et al., 2016; Owen et al., 2013; Xiao et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature on OXT effects on neuronal activity.

claims.claim: OXT selectively increases MeA responses to female stimuli.
claims.source: OXT selectively increases MeA responses to female stimuli, indicating that OXT signaling has the ability to differentially modulate the specific sensing of female cues through its action on MeA neurons co-expressing aromatase and OXTR.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological recording data showing selective enhancement of female responses.

claims.claim: OXT signaling has the ability to differentially modulate the specific sensing of female cues through its action on MeA neurons co-expressing aromatase and OXTR.

claims.claim: The MeA receives direct sensory input from the AOB.
claims.source: The MeA receives direct sensory input from the AOB and is reciprocally connected with hypothalamic behavior centers.
claims.evidence: This claim draws from established scientific knowledge about MeA connectivity.

claims.claim: The MeA is reciprocally connected with hypothalamic behavior centers.
claims.source: The MeA receives direct sensory input from the AOB and is reciprocally connected with hypothalamic behavior centers.
claims.evidence: This claim draws from established scientific knowledge about MeA connectivity.

claims.claim: Sex-specific sensory cues are relayed separately at the receptor level.
claims.source: Although sex-specific sensory cues are relayed separately at the receptor level, AOB mitral cells, which send input to MeA neurons, often respond to multiple sensory stimuli.

claims.claim: AOB mitral cells often respond to multiple sensory stimuli.

claims.evidence: This claim is speculative, proposing a possible mechanism for OXT specificity.

claims.claim: The specificity of OXT in modulating female-evoked neural responses may be achieved by regulating the local MeA circuitry.
claims.source: Alternatively, the specificity of OXT in modulating female-evoked neural responses may be achieved by regulating the local MeA circuitry, for example by acting on a specific set of local aromatase- and OXTR-expressing interneurons that boost responses to female cues while dampening responses to male and predator signals.
claims.evidence: This claim is speculative, proposing an alternative mechanism for OXT specificity.

claims.claim: By dynamically and selectively tuning the neural representation of social cues in a genetically defined neuronal population of the MeA, OXT may alter the behavioral significance of social stimuli on a moment-to-moment basis.
claims.source: Thus, by dynamically and selectively tuning the neural representation of social cues in a genetically defined neuronal population of the MeA, OXT may alter the behavioral significance of social stimuli on a moment-to-moment basis.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the combined behavioral and electrophysiological data showing acute OXT effects.

claims.claim: MeA units in male mice with wild-type OXTR function were most responsive to female (23.6%) and predator (13.2%) cues, while less than 1% of MeA units from control males responded to male stimuli.
claims.source: In accord with previous c-fos and electrophysiological findings (Bergan et al., 2014; Choi et al., 2005; Kang et al., 2011; Samuelsen and Meredith, 2009), MeA units in male mice with wild-type OXTR function were most responsive to female (23.6%) and predator (13.2%) cues, while less than 1% of MeA units from control males responded to male stimuli (Figure 4D–G).

claims.claim: In male mice lacking OXT signaling in the aromatase-expressing neurons, the proportion of MeA units responsive to female stimuli was reduced (6.2%), while the proportions of units responsive to male (6.7%) and predator (23.3%) stimuli were increased compared to control male mice.
claims.source: By contrast, in male mice lacking OXT signaling in the aromatase-expressing neurons, the proportion of MeA units responsive to female stimuli was reduced (6.2%), while the proportions of units responsive to male (6.7%) and predator (23.3%) stimuli were increased compared to control male mice (Figure 4D).

claims.claim: The observed difference in response rates between control mice and male mice lacking OXT signaling in the aromatase-expressing neurons was significant for each stimulus.

claims.claim: The average response strength of predator neurons was reduced by ~10% in mutant male mice as compared to control male mice.
claims.source: We found that the response strength (spikes/second) to conspecific cues was not dramatically changed by permanent loss of OXT signaling although the average response strength of predator neurons was reduced by ~10% in mutant male mice as compared to control male mice (Figure 4E; p<0.05).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological recording data presented in Figure 4E.

claims.claim: The inability to discriminate sex-specific cues observed in mice with impaired OXT signaling coincides with a clear reorganization of sensory responses to social stimuli in the MeA.

claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the correlation between behavioral and electrophysiological phenotypes.

claims.claim: OXTR antagonist administration specifically reduced the time that male mice spent in the female interaction zone.
claims.source: We found that OXTR antagonist administration specifically reduced the time that male mice spent in the female interaction zone (Figure 5A–B), without affecting the time spent in the male interaction zone or the total distance travelled (saline: female interaction zone = 159.8 ± 18.1 s, male interaction zone = 93.8 ± 8.9 s; p<0.001; preference score = 0.24 ± 0.04, total distance travelled = 3709 ± 160 cm; OXTR antagonist: female interaction zone = 106.4 ± 11.0 s, male interaction zone = 101.6 ± 12.7 s; p=0.79; preference score = 0.04 ± 0.08, total distance travelled = 3360 ± 247 cm; n = 12; Figure 5C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data presented in Figure 5A-C.

claims.claim: The changes at the behavioral level could be observed 30 min after IP injection of OXTR antagonist.
claims.source: The changes at the behavioral level could be observed 30 min after IP injection, demonstrating that normal social interactions with conspecifics rely on OXT signaling in adults and that acute modulation in OXT signaling can promptly modify behavioral responses.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the timing of behavioral changes following drug injection.

claims.claim: Normal social interactions with conspecifics rely on OXT signaling in adults.

claims.claim: Acute modulation in OXT signaling can promptly modify behavioral responses.

claims.claim: In the absence of sensory stimulation, injection of the OXTR antagonist decreased the firing rate of MeA units.

claims.claim: OXTR antagonist reduced the number of neuronal responses categorized as 'female'.

claims.claim: OXTR antagonist increased the number of neuronal responses categorized as 'male'.

claims.claim: OXTR antagonist increased the number of neuronal responses categorized as 'predator'.

claims.evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological recording data presented in Figure 5G.

claims.claim: OXTR antagonist application dramatically reduced the strength of female-responsive units.
claims.source: OXTR antagonist application dramatically reduced the strength of female-responsive units (p=0.003; Wilcoxon signed rank test; Figure 5H, red), modestly increased the strength of male-responsive units (p=0.07; Wilcoxon signed rank test; Figure 5H, blue), and showed no clear effect on predator responsive units (p=1; Wilcoxon signed rank test; Figure 5H, green).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological recording data presented in Figure 5H.

claims.claim: The reduced response to female stimuli is the major effect of OXTR antagonist in the MeA.
claims.source: Moreover, in view of the decrease in response strength to female stimuli following OXTR antagonist (Figure 5H), but not males or predators, it is clear that the reduced response to female stimuli is the major effect of OXTR antagonist in the MeA.

claims.claim: OXT-expressing neurons in the PVN are the major contributor of OXT fibers in all 27 brain areas examined.
claims.source: Consistent with previous reports (Buijs et al., 1983; Knobloch et al., 2012), our results show that OXT-expressing neurons in the PVN, but not those in the SON, are the major contributor of OXT fibers in all 27 brain areas examined (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by anatomical mapping data presented in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Medium to high levels of OXT fibers originated from the PVN can be found in the BNST and MeA.
claims.source: Medium to high levels of OXT fibers originated from the PVN can be found in the BNST and MeA, two chemosensory nuclei with dense populations of aromatase-expressing neurons, whereas only sparse OXT fibers from the SON were found in the two areas.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by anatomical mapping data.

claims.evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data presented in Figure 6D-E.

claims.claim: Direct modulation of the neuronal source of OXT in the PVN can lead to fast and reversible changes in social interaction preference.
claims.source: Thus, direct modulation of the neuronal source of OXT in the PVN can lead to fast and reversible changes in social interaction preference.

claims.claim: OXT-iCre mice with DREADD virus infection in the SON did not show any significant change in social interaction after CNO injection.

claims.claim: IP injection of CNO caused intense self-grooming in Oxt-iCre mice expressing excitatory DREADD in the PVN OXT-expressing neurons.
claims.source: Indeed, IP injection of CNO caused intense self-grooming in Oxt-iCre mice expressing excitatory DREADD in the PVN OXT-expressing neurons, indicating acute elevation of central OXT signaling.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral observations following CNO injection.

claims.claim: Oxt-iCre mice expressing excitatory DREADD in the PVN showed a loss preference for female stimuli when tested 15 min after CNO injection.
claims.source: When tested 15 min after CNO injection, that is after the phase of intense grooming had subsided, Oxt-iCre mice expressing excitatory DREADD in the PVN showed a loss preference for female stimuli (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A), which did not recover 2 days, 1 week and even 2 weeks post CNO injection (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B–C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data presented in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: CNO modestly increased the firing rate of MeA units in the absence of sensory stimulation.
claims.source: CNO modestly increased the firing rate of MeA units in the absence of sensory stimulation (Figure 7E).

claims.claim: OXT activation by CNO increased the number of neuronal responses categorized as 'female'.
claims.source: We found that the OXT activation by CNO increased the number of neuronal responses categorized as 'female' (Figure 7G; 16.9% responding before; 29.3% responding after; p<=0.03, permutation test), modestly decreased the number of neuronal responses categorized as 'male' (3.8% responding before; 0.0% responding after; p<=0.069, permutation test), and had little effect on the number of neurons categorized as predator (12.3% responding before; 10.3%).

claims.claim: CNO injection increased the strength of female-responsive units.
claims.source: CNO injection increased the strength of female-responsive units (p=0.0005; Wilcoxon signed rank test; Figure 7H, red), while having little effect on the response strength of male (p=0.63; Wilcoxon signed rank test) or predator (p=0.82; Wilcoxon signed rank test) evoked neural responses.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological recording data presented in Figure 7H.

claims.source: These findings suggest that DREADD activation initially impacted MeA responses strongly, but led to a subsequent inactivation of OXT signaling.

results.result: OXT knockout male mice lose their typical preference for female conspecifics in social interaction and chemosensory investigation assays. Oxt-/- males show no significant preference for investigating females over males, while wild-type males spend significantly more time investigating females. Total investigation time remains similar between genotypes, indicating the deficit is specific to sex discrimination rather than general social interest.
results.evaluation: Claims C33-C40 provide converging behavioral evidence from multiple assays (3-chamber social interaction and bedding investigation) with appropriate statistical tests showing loss of female preference in OXT mutants while maintaining normal total investigation time. The data include proper controls (empty cups/chambers) and adequate sample sizes (n=9-13).

results.result: Loss of OXT does not significantly affect odor preference in female mice. Both Oxt+/+ and Oxt-/- females show similar slight preferences for female bedding, and no preference is observed in females at different estrous cycle stages.
results.evaluation: Claims C41-C43 demonstrate sex-specific effects of OXT with appropriate statistical comparisons between genotypes and estrous stages. The data show consistent lack of OXT effect in females across multiple conditions, supporting the specificity of OXT function in male social preference.

results.result: OXT mutant mice retain normal responses to predator cues and can detect and remember conspecific odors through habituation/dishabituation. Both wild-type and OXT mutant males avoid fox urine and show normal habituation to repeated same-sex urine followed by dishabituation to opposite-sex urine.
results.evaluation: Claims C44-C49 provide important control experiments demonstrating that OXT loss specifically affects social preference processing rather than general sensory detection, predator avoidance, or memory. The Y-maze and habituation/dishabituation assays with appropriate statistical tests support this specificity.

results.result: The effect of OXT on sex-specific chemosensory preference is mediated exclusively by OXTR, not by vasopressin receptors. Male mice lacking V1aR, V1bR, or both receptors show normal preference for female chemostimuli, while OXT mutants do not.
results.evaluation: Claims C50-C53 provide clear genetic dissection showing that despite cross-reactivity between OXT and AVP systems, the behavioral phenotype is specific to OXTR. Multiple AVP receptor knockout lines (V1aR, V1bR, double knockout) all show normal female preference with appropriate statistical comparisons.

results.result: OXT signaling in aromatase-expressing neurons of the MeApd is necessary for sex discrimination. Genetic ablation of OXTR in Cyp19a1-Cre neurons eliminates female preference in both social interaction and bedding investigation assays, while ablation in TRH neurons does not affect this behavior.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C60-C65 demonstrate cell-type-specific requirement using conditional knockout approaches with appropriate Cre lines. The data show loss of female preference specifically with aromatase-Cre but not TRH-Cre ablation, with normal predator avoidance maintained, supporting anatomical and molecular specificity.

results.result: Virus-mediated manipulation of OXTR in adult MeA, but not BNST, is both necessary and sufficient for sex discrimination. AAV-Cre injection in MeA of Oxtrflox/flox mice eliminates female preference, while AAV-OXTR injection in MeA of Cyp19a1-Cre;Oxtrflox/flox mice rescues the phenotype. Neither manipulation in BNST affects behavior.
results.evaluation: Claims C66-C72 provide strong anatomical specificity through virus-mediated loss-of-function and gain-of-function experiments in adult mice. The bidirectional manipulations with appropriate controls (GFP virus, BNST targeting) and statistical tests support MeA as the critical site for OXT action.

results.result: OXT signaling acts acutely in adults rather than developmentally to regulate sex discrimination. Virus-mediated ablation and rescue of OXTR in adult MeA produce corresponding behavioral changes, and similar phenotypes are observed in constitutive and conditional adult manipulations.
results.evaluation: Claims C73-C74, C79-C80 address the critical developmental versus acute function question. The virus-mediated manipulations in adults producing rapid behavioral changes, combined with consistency across constitutive and conditional approaches, strongly support acute adult function rather than developmental organization.

results.result: Loss of OXT signaling in aromatase-expressing neurons causes reorganization of MeA sensory responses. In mutants, the proportion of neurons responding to female stimuli decreases from 23.6% to 6.2%, while responses to male stimuli increase from <1% to 6.7%. Response strength to conspecific cues is largely maintained, though predator responses are modestly reduced.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C75-C78, C103-C107 provide electrophysiological evidence linking behavioral phenotype to altered neural representations. The single-unit recording data with appropriate statistical tests (permutation tests, p≤0.02 for all stimuli) show clear reorganization of sensory responses that parallels behavioral deficits.

results.result: Acute pharmacological blockade of OXTR with antagonist rapidly eliminates male preference for females and alters MeA neural responses. Within 30 minutes of antagonist injection, males lose female preference, baseline MeA firing decreases, female-responsive neurons decrease from 16.4% to 3.3%, and female response strength is dramatically reduced.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C108-C117 demonstrate acute necessity of OXT signaling through pharmacological manipulation with parallel behavioral and electrophysiological measurements. The rapid time course (30 min), specific reduction in female responses, and appropriate statistical tests (permutation tests, Wilcoxon signed rank) strongly support acute modulation.

results.result: OXT neurons in the PVN, but not SON, are the major source of OXT fibers to MeA and mediate sex discrimination behavior. Anatomical mapping shows PVN provides medium-high OXT fiber density to MeA while SON provides sparse fibers. Chemogenetic inhibition of PVN OXT neurons eliminates female preference for 1 hour to 2 days with recovery by 1 week, while SON inhibition has no effect.
results.evaluation: Claims C118-C126 identify the source of OXT through anatomical tracing and functional manipulation. The DREADD experiments with appropriate controls (saline injection, SON targeting) and time course analysis demonstrate PVN as the critical source. The reversibility supports acute neuromodulatory function.

results.result: Chemogenetic activation of PVN OXT neurons initially enhances female-responsive MeA neurons but leads to subsequent long-lasting behavioral deficits. CNO injection causes intense grooming, increases female-responsive neurons from 16.9% to 29.3% and their response strength, but results in loss of female preference lasting at least 2 weeks, possibly due to OXT depletion or receptor desensitization.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C127-C135 show complex biphasic effects that are difficult to interpret. While the initial enhancement of female responses is clear (C130-C131), the paradoxical long-lasting behavioral deficit (C128) contradicts the expected outcome. The proposed mechanisms (C135) are speculative. The disconnect between acute neural enhancement and prolonged behavioral impairment requires further investigation to resolve.

results.result: OXT signaling in aromatase-expressing MeA neurons modulates behavioral and neural responses to female cues on a moment-to-moment basis by selectively enhancing female-evoked responses while suppressing male and predator responses. This filtering mechanism alters the behavioral significance of social stimuli according to context.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C86-C89, C94-C95, C102 synthesize the major findings into a coherent model. The parallel changes in neural responses and behavior, combined with acute reversibility and cell-type specificity, support moment-to-moment modulation. However, the mechanistic details of how OXT achieves stimulus-selective enhancement remain to be fully elucidated.

results.result: Background claims establishing the general properties of neuropeptide signaling, OXT/AVP function in social behaviors, and the role of the vomeronasal system and MeA in processing social chemosensory cues.
results.evaluation: Claims C7-C32 provide established background knowledge supported by appropriate citations to previous literature. These claims set the context for the current study and are generally well-accepted in the field based on prior work.

results.result: Anatomical and molecular characterization of MeA subdivisions relevant to the study. The MeA expresses OXTR, receives AOB input, shows topographically organized responses, and contains distinct populations expressing TRH (MeApv) and aromatase (MeApd).
results.evaluation: Claims C54-C59 provide anatomical context supported by citations and established knowledge. These claims justify the focus on specific MeA subpopulations and are well-supported by prior literature.

results.result: Discussion claims contextualizing the findings within prior work on steroid organization of MeA circuits, OXT regulation, and mechanisms of OXT action including effects on neurotransmitter release and neuronal firing.
results.evaluation: Claims C81-C85, C90-C93 provide appropriate context from prior literature to interpret the current findings. The distinction between organizational effects of steroids (C81) and acute OXT modulation (C82) is well-supported by the data. The mechanistic possibilities (C92-C93) are appropriately cited.

results.result: Discussion of MeA circuit organization and speculative mechanisms for OXT specificity. The MeA receives AOB input and projects to hypothalamus. Possible mechanisms for female-specific OXT effects include preferential connectivity from female-responsive AOB neurons or local circuit regulation.
results.evaluation: Claims C96-C99 state established anatomical facts, but C100-C101 are explicitly speculative about mechanisms underlying OXT specificity. These hypotheses are reasonable but lack direct experimental support in the current study. Future work is needed to distinguish between these possibilities.
